extracted.intended_audience: science communication researchers and practitioners (e.g., university press officers, science journalists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for writing science press releases to maximize journalistic pickup, based on Schäfer's mediatization review: emphasize news-values (conflict, novelty, personalization, narrative) while preserving scientific quality. Useful for press officers and communicators aiming to improve media attention for scientific findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mediatization (core diagnostic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mediatization means science coverage increasingly follows journalistic news values rather than scientific ones: conflict, novelty, personalization, narrative arc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A science press release that doesn't recognize this pattern under-performs even when scientifically excellent. Releases should package scientific findings in terms journalists expect so the scientific quality can reach the journalist via a journalistic-value envelope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release surface a tension or controversy (within the field, between fields, with public expectation, with regulation) the journalist can build a story around?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists favor stories with visible tensions; pure consensus releases are picked up less. Frame findings in relation to a debate, disagreement, regulatory tension, or public expectation to create a hook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release explicitly mark what is new relative to prior science? Use concrete claims like 'First study to', 'Largest cohort to date', 'First evidence in humans' rather than vague claims of importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit, verifiable novelty claims increase pickup. Avoid vague or generic statements of importance; quantify or qualify novelty where possible (first, largest, strongest evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization hook
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release name an individual researcher (with quotable role) or an affected individual (patient, community member)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mediatized coverage requires personalization. Provide named, quotable people (researchers or those affected) to create human-interest angles and soundbites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative arc
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release fit a recognizable story shape (puzzle → discovery; problem → solution; expectation → surprise)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Releases with a clear narrative arc are easier for journalists to turn into stories. Use familiar story structures to present background, tension, the finding, and implications; releases lacking an arc are harder to publish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility of controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release acknowledge dissenting views and the scientific debate the finding enters?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledging counterarguments or ongoing debate satisfies journalists' balance norms and increases credibility and pickup. Explicitly situate findings within existing controversies rather than presenting them as uncontested fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual-friendly framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release provide visuals (images of researchers, sample images, animations, or infographics) with clear usage rights?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mediatized science requires visuals; supplying high-quality, cleared visuals (and clear usage/licensing information) makes a release more attractive to media outlets and multiplatform coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary salience differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the disciplinary factors that affect coverage acknowledged? Some fields (medicine, climate, neuroscience) systematically get more coverage than others (mathematics, theoretical physics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Releases from low-coverage fields need stronger novelty and narrative work to compete. Tailor framing to compensate for disciplinary differences in journalistic interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue-attention cycle awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release land at a moment when the news cycle is attending to the topic (awareness of the issue-attention curve)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pickup is highest when the release coincides with existing media attention. Timing and topicality matter — releases that anticipate or align with the issue-attention cycle outperform those that do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of deficit-model framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release avoid lecturing the public ('the public must understand that...') and instead meet the public on its terms?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Releases framed as public lectures underperform. Communicate findings in accessible, relevant terms rather than assuming a knowledge deficit in the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust-building over single-event impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release treat each communication as part of a long-term trust relationship rather than relying on one-off blockbusters?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schäfer's review supports building sustained trust: prioritizing accuracy and consistency over sensational single-event gains preserves future pickup. One-off blockbusters that sacrifice accuracy can reduce future media receptivity.
